questions.q: Let $p=(x+y+z)$ and $q=xyz$. If $\begin{vmatrix} x \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } y \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } z \end{vmatrix}$ is positive, then which one of the following is correct ?
questions.solution:
Expanding the given determinant along the first row and setting it greater than zero:

$x(yz - 1) - 1(z - 1) + 1(1 - y) > 0$

$xyz - x - z + 1 + 1 - y > 0$

$xyz - (x + y + z) + 2 > 0$

Substituting $p = x + y + z$ and $q = xyz$:

$q - p + 2 > 0$

$q + 2 > p$

Answer: $q+2 > p$

questions.q: The system of equations $2x - 3y - 5 = 0$, $15y - 10x + 50 = 0$
options: is consistent and has exactly two solutions
questions.solution:
The given system of equations is:
$2x - 3y - 5 = 0$
$-10x + 15y + 50 = 0$

Comparing with $a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0$, we have:
$a_1 = 2$, $b_1 = -3$, $c_1 = -5$
$a_2 = -10$, $b_2 = 15$, $c_2 = 50$

Calculating the ratios of the coefficients:
$\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{-10} = -\dfrac{1}{5}$

$\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{5}$

$\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-5}{50} = -\dfrac{1}{10}$

Since $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$, the lines represented by the equations are parallel and distinct.

Thus, the system of equations has no solution and is inconsistent.

questions.q: Let $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 3x^2 \text{ and } \cos x \text{ and } -\sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$ where $q$ is any constant, then what is $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\big(f(x)\big)$ at $x=0$ equal to ?
questions.solution:
Given the function $f(x)$ as a determinant where only the first row contains the variable $x$:

$f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 3x^2 \text{ and } \cos x \text{ and } -\sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

To differentiate the determinant with respect to $x$, we differentiate the elements of the first row while keeping the other rows unchanged.

Differentiating once with respect to $x$:

$f'(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 6x \text{ and } -\sin x \text{ and } -\cos x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Differentiating again with respect to $x$:

$f''(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 6 \text{ and } -\cos x \text{ and } \sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Substituting $x=0$ into the second derivative:

$f''(0)=\begin{vmatrix} 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Since the first and second rows of the determinant are identical, the value of the determinant is zero.

$f''(0) = 0$

Answer: $0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $M=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, then what is the value of $|M|\,|\text{adj}M|$ ?
questions.solution:
Given $M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of the diagonal matrix $M$ is $|M| = 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.

For a square matrix of order $n$, the determinant of its adjoint is given by $|\text{adj}M| = |M|^{n-1}$.

Since the order of $M$ is $n = 3$, we have $|\text{adj}M| = |M|^{3-1} = |M|^2$.

The required value is $|M| \, |\text{adj}M| = |M| \times |M|^2 = |M|^3$.

Substituting $|M| = 8$, we get $8^3 = 512$.

Answer: $512$

questions.q: If $\begin{vmatrix} a-b \text{ and } p-q \text{ and } x-y \\ b-c \text{ and } q-r \text{ and } y-z \\ c-a \text{ and } r-p \text{ and } z-x \end{vmatrix}=k\begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ x \text{ and } y \text{ and } z \end{vmatrix}$, then what is the value of $k$ ?
questions.solution:
Let $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a-b \text{ and } p-q \text{ and } x-y \\ b-c \text{ and } q-r \text{ and } y-z \\ c-a \text{ and } r-p \text{ and } z-x \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the row operation $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, we get:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} (a-b)+(b-c)+(c-a) \text{ and } (p-q)+(q-r)+(r-p) \text{ and } (x-y)+(y-z)+(z-x) \\ b-c \text{ and } q-r \text{ and } y-z \\ c-a \text{ and } r-p \text{ and } z-x \end{vmatrix}$

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 \text{ and } 0 \text{ and } 0 \\ b-c \text{ and } q-r \text{ and } y-z \\ c-a \text{ and } r-p \text{ and } z-x \end{vmatrix}$

Since all elements of the first row are zero, the value of the determinant is $0$.

Comparing this with $k\begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ x \text{ and } y \text{ and } z \end{vmatrix}$, we get $k = 0$.

questions.q: $The value of the determinant \begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \end{vmatrix}$ is equal to
options: $\begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix}$
$\begin{vmatrix} l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \end{vmatrix}$
$\begin{vmatrix} p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix}$
$\begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } p \text{ and } l \\ b \text{ and } q \text{ and } m \\ c \text{ and } r \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix}$
questions.solution:
Let $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \\ p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \end{vmatrix}$

Interchanging the first and third rows (R_1 \leftrightarrow R_3$), the sign of the determinant changes:

\Delta = -\begin{vmatrix} p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \end{vmatrix}$

Now, interchanging the second and third rows (R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3$), the sign changes again:

\Delta = -\left( -\begin{vmatrix} p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix} \right) = \begin{vmatrix} p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{vmatrix} p \text{ and } q \text{ and } r \\ a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ l \text{ and } m \text{ and } n \end{vmatrix}$

questions.q: If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle $ABC$ and $p$ is the perimeter of the triangle, then what is $\begin{vmatrix} p+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$ equal to?
questions.solution:
Let $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} p+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the column operation $C_1 \rightarrow C_1 + C_2 + C_3$:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} p+a+b+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ p+a+b+c \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ p+a+b+c \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Since $p = a+b+c$ is the perimeter of the triangle, we have $p+a+b+c = 2p$. Substituting this into the determinant:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2p \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 2p \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ 2p \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Taking $2p$ common from the first column $C_1$:

$\Delta = 2p \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } p+a \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } p+b \end{vmatrix}$

Applying the row operations $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_1$:

$\Delta = 2p \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } a \text{ and } b \\ 0 \text{ and } p \text{ and } 0 \\ 0 \text{ and } 0 \text{ and } p \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first column $C_1$:

$\Delta = 2p [1(p \cdot p - 0)] = 2p(p^2) = 2p^3$

Answer: $2p^3$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: If $X$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then $\det(mX) = m^n \det(X)$, where $m$ is a scalar.
Statement-II: If $Y$ is a matrix obtained from $X$ by multiplying any row or column by a scalar $m$, then $\det(Y) = m\det(X)$.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is not correct
Statement-I is not correct but Statement-II is correct
questions.solution:
Statement-I states that for an $n \times n$ matrix $X$, $\det(mX) = m^n \det(X)$. This is a standard property of determinants and is correct.

Statement-II states that if a single row or column of a matrix is multiplied by a scalar $m$, the determinant of the resulting matrix is $m$ times the determinant of the original matrix. This is also a fundamental property of determinants and is correct.

Multiplying a matrix $X$ by a scalar $m$ is equivalent to multiplying each of its $n$ rows by $m$. By applying the property given in Statement-II $n$ times (once for each row), we can factor out $m$ from each of the $n$ rows, yielding $m^n \det(X)$.

Thus, Statement-II provides the logical reasoning required to prove Statement-I. Both statements are correct, and Statement-II explains Statement-I.

questions.q: If $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a \text{ and } b \text{ and } c \\ d \text{ and } e \text{ and } f \\ g \text{ and } h \text{ and } i \end{vmatrix}$ and $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $G$ are the cofactors of the elements $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $g$ respectively, then what is $bB + cC - dD - gG$ equal to?
questions.solution:
The sum of the products of elements of any row or column with their corresponding cofactors is equal to the determinant $\Delta$.

Expanding the determinant along the first row, we get:
$aA + bB + cC = \Delta$

Expanding the determinant along the first column, we get:
$aA + dD + gG = \Delta$

Subtracting the second equation from the first equation, we get:
$(aA + bB + cC) - (aA + dD + gG) = \Delta - \Delta$

$bB + cC - dD - gG = 0$

Answer: $0$

questions.q: If $A^2 + B^2 + C^2 = 0$, then what is the value of $\begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } \cos C \text{ and } \cos B \\ \cos C \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } \cos A \\ \cos B \text{ and } \cos A \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix}$?
questions.solution:
Given $A^2 + B^2 + C^2 = 0$.

Since the square of any real number is non-negative, the sum of squares can be zero if and only if each number is zero.

Thus, $A = 0$, $B = 0$, and $C = 0$.

Substituting these values into the determinant, we get $\cos A = \cos 0 = 1$, $\cos B = \cos 0 = 1$, and $\cos C = \cos 0 = 1$.

The given determinant becomes:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Since all rows are identical, the value of the determinant is 0$.

Answer: 0$

questions.q:
Consider the following statements in respect of the determinant $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} k(k+2) \text{ and } 2k+1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 2k+1 \text{ and } k+2 \text{ and } 1 \\ 3 \text{ and } 3 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix}$:
I. $\Delta$ is positive if $k > 0$.
II. $\Delta$ is negative if $k < 0$.
III. $\Delta$ is zero if $k = 0$.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.solution:
Given determinant is $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} k(k+2) \text{ and } 2k+1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 2k+1 \text{ and } k+2 \text{ and } 1 \\ 3 \text{ and } 3 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Applying row operations $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$ and $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_3$:

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} k^2-1 \text{ and } k-1 \text{ and } 0 \\ 2k-2 \text{ and } k-1 \text{ and } 0 \\ 3 \text{ and } 3 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along the third column:

$\Delta = 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} k^2-1 \text{ and } k-1 \\ 2k-2 \text{ and } k-1 \end{vmatrix}$

$\Delta = (k^2-1)(k-1) - (2k-2)(k-1)$

$\Delta = (k-1) [ k^2 - 1 - 2k + 2 ]$

$\Delta = (k-1) (k^2 - 2k + 1)$

$\Delta = (k-1)^3$

Evaluating the given statements:

I. For $k = \dfrac{1}{2} > 0$, $\Delta = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - 1\right)^3 = -\dfrac{1}{8} < 0$. Thus, statement I is incorrect.

II. For $k < 0$, $k - 1 < -1$, which implies $(k-1)^3 < 0$. Thus, statement II is correct.

III. For $k = 0$, $\Delta = (0-1)^3 = -1 \neq 0$. Thus, statement III is incorrect.

Only one statement is correct.

Answer: One

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\begin{vmatrix}$2 & 3+i & -1 \\ 3-i & 0 & i-1 \\ -1 & -1-i & 1 \end{vmatrix} = A + iB$ where $i = $\sqrt{-1}, then what is $A + B$ equal to?$
questions.solution:
Given the determinant:

$\begin{vmatrix} 2 \text{ and } 3+i \text{ and } -1 \\ 3-i \text{ and } 0 \text{ and } i-1 \\ -1 \text{ and } -1-i \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = A + iB$

Expanding the determinant along the first row, we get:

$D = 2 \begin{vmatrix} 0 \text{ and } i-1 \\ -1-i \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} - (3+i) \begin{vmatrix} 3-i \text{ and } i-1 \\ -1 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} - 1 \begin{vmatrix} 3-i \text{ and } 0 \\ -1 \text{ and } -1-i \end{vmatrix}$

Evaluating each $2 \times 2$ minor:

First minor:
$\begin{vmatrix} 0 \text{ and } i-1 \\ -1-i \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = (0)(1) - (i-1)(-1-i) = 0 - (-(i^2 - 1)) = 0 - (-(-1 - 1)) = -2$

Second minor:
$\begin{vmatrix} 3-i \text{ and } i-1 \\ -1 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = (3-i)(1) - (i-1)(-1) = 3 - i + i - 1 = 2$

Third minor:
$\begin{vmatrix} 3-i \text{ and } 0 \\ -1 \text{ and } -1-i \end{vmatrix} = (3-i)(-1-i) - (0)(-1) = -3 - 3i + i + i^2 = -3 - 2i - 1 = -4 - 2i$

Substituting these values back into the expansion:

$D = 2(-2) - (3+i)(2) - 1(-4 - 2i)$

$D = -4 - (6 + 2i) + (4 + 2i)$

$D = -4 - 6 - 2i + 4 + 2i$

$D = -6$

Comparing this with $A + iB$, we get:
$A = -6$ and $B = 0$

Therefore, $A + B = -6 + 0 = -6$.

Answer: $-6$

questions.q:
Consider the following in respect of a non-singular matrix $M$:
I. $|M^2| = |M|^2$
II. $|M| = |M^{-1}|$
III. $|M| = |M^T|$
How many of the above are correct?
questions.solution:
For a non-singular matrix $M$, $|M| \neq 0$.

Using the property of determinants $|AB| = |A||B|$, we have $|M^2| = |M \cdot M| = |M||M| = |M|^2$. Thus, Statement I is correct.

Using the property $M M^{-1} = I$, taking the determinant on both sides gives $|M M^{-1}| = |I| \Rightarrow |M||M^{-1}| = 1 \Rightarrow |M^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|M|}$. Since $|M|$ is not necessarily equal to $\dfrac{1}{|M|}$, Statement II is incorrect.

The determinant of a matrix is always equal to the determinant of its transpose, so $|M| = |M^T|$. Thus, Statement III is correct.

Exactly two of the given statements are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.q: If $\mathrm{D}_n=\left|\begin{array}{lll}n & 20 & 30 \\ n^2 & 40 & 50 \\ n^3 & 60 & 70\end{array}\right|$ then what is the value of $\sum_{n=1}^4 \mathrm{D}_n$ ?
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned} & D_n=\left|\begin{array}{lll}n & 20 & 30 \\ n^2 & 40 & 50 \\ n^3 & 60 & 70\end{array}\right|=(20)(10)\left|\begin{array}{lll}n & 1 & 3 \\ n^2 & 2 & 5 \\ n^3 & 3 & 7\end{array}\right| \\ & \Rightarrow D_n=200\left[n(14-15)-1\left(7 n^2-5 n^3\right)+3\left(3 n^2-2 n^3\right)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow D_n=200\left(-n+2 n^2-n^3\right)\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Now, } \sum_{n=1}^4 D_n=200 \sum_{n=1}^4\left(-n+2 n^2-n^3\right) \\
& \because \sum n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \sum n^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6} \\
& \sum n^3=\left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2
\end{aligned}$
Hence,
$\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{n=1}^4 D_n=200\left[-\frac{(4)(5)}{2}+2 \cdot \frac{(4)(5)(9)}{6}-\left(\frac{(4)(5)}{2}\right)^2\right] \\
& =200(-50)=-10000
\end{aligned}$

Since the determinant of a matrix is equal to the determinant of its transpose, $|A^{\text{T}}| = |A|$.

Substituting this into the equation gives $|AA^{\text{T}}| = |A||A| = |A|^2$.

Given $|A| = -2$, we get $|AA^{\text{T}}| = (-2)^2 = 4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.q: In obtaining the solution of the system of equations $x + y + z = 7$, $x + 2y + 3z = 16$ and $x + 3y + 4z = 22$ by Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is obtained by dividing $D$ by $D_2$, where $D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } 2 \text{ and } 3 \\ 1 \text{ and } 3 \text{ and } 4 \end{vmatrix}$. What is the value of the determinant $D_2$?
questions.solution:
The given system of linear equations is:
$x + y + z = 7$
$x + 2y + 3z = 16$
$x + 3y + 4z = 22$

By Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y = \dfrac{D_2}{D}$, where $D_2$ is the determinant obtained by replacing the second column of the coefficient matrix $D$ with the column of constant terms.

$D_2 = \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 7 \text{ and } 1 \\ 1 \text{ and } 16 \text{ and } 3 \\ 1 \text{ and } 22 \text{ and } 4 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:
$D_2 = 1(16 \times 4 - 3 \times 22) - 7(1 \times 4 - 3 \times 1) + 1(1 \times 22 - 16 \times 1)$

$D_2 = 1(64 - 66) - 7(4 - 3) + 1(22 - 16)$

$D_2 = 1(-2) - 7(1) + 1(6)$

$D_2 = -2 - 7 + 6$

$D_2 = -3$

Answer: $-3$

\end{aligned}$
